title: How T20 Cricket Changed the Game Forever — For Better and For Worse
summary: Twenty years after T20 cricket was introduced to international schedules, we assess its extraordinary impact on the sport — the new audiences it created, the players it produced, and the traditions it has challenged.
content:
Cricket in 2006 looked nothing like cricket in 2026. The game has been transformed by Twenty20 — a format that was dismissed by traditionalists as a gimmick, celebrated by administrators as a commercial lifeline, and has ultimately become the most popular and most lucrative version of the sport on the planet.

Assessing what T20 has done to cricket requires holding two things simultaneously in mind: the genuine good it has produced, and the genuine problems it has created. Neither picture is complete without the other.

What T20 Did Right

T20 brought new audiences to cricket. In India — always the sport's most important market — the IPL became a cultural event that rivals the most popular entertainment properties in one of the world's largest countries. Players who had never watched cricket became fans. Young people who found Test matches too long, too slow, too demanding of their attention had a version of the game that demanded nothing more than three hours.

T20 also democratised excellence. Teams from non-traditional cricket nations — Afghanistan, Nepal, Namibia — found that the shorter format gave them a genuine chance to compete with established powers. The World T20 has produced results — Afghanistan beating Pakistan, Scotland running India close — that simply could not have happened at any other level of the sport.

The Financial Revolution

The IPL's commercial model — franchise cricket, with city-based teams, overseas player auctions, and broadcast deals worth billions — created wealth that has flowed through cricket at every level. Players from associate nations can now earn enough to pursue cricket professionally. Academies in non-traditional markets receive funding. The sport's financial base has expanded enormously.

T20 gave cricket a future. Without it, the sport would have continued declining in relevance — particularly among young people. The format is not perfect, but it saved cricket's commercial viability, and that matters. — Former ICC Chairman

What T20 Has Cost

The honest accounting of T20's impact must include what has been lost or diminished. Test cricket — the game's highest form, its most demanding, its most rewarding for those patient enough to follow it — has struggled in some markets as the financial and scheduling pressures of T20 leagues have grown.

Players from non-Indian boards face pressure to prioritise franchise T20 cricket over national commitments. Some of the game's best players have retired from international cricket earlier than previous generations to pursue franchise contracts. The technique required for Test cricket — the defence, the patience, the ability to build an innings across hours — is practiced less, valued less, and perhaps understood less by a generation raised on the hitting-first philosophy of T20.

The Coexistence Question

Can Test cricket and T20 cricket coexist indefinitely? The ICC and most cricket administrators say yes. The evidence from some markets is less encouraging. England's domestic structure has adapted — the Hundred, whatever its controversies, has brought new fans to cricket. India's market is healthy enough to support both formats. Australia maintains strong Test attendance.

But the pressure is real and growing. The sport's administrators face choices in the coming decade that will determine whether the richness of cricket's full range of formats survives, or whether the market ultimately decides that three hours is enough.
